rv.q: She pulls it off with power and finesse.
Stori Ayers keeps her cast almost airborne — the speed is so intense that the few moments of stillness hit the audience like brick walls.
Feels like an elegant experiment, thoughtful and put-together but not quite realizing its full potential.
"Confederates" itself has some loops in its tone, and holes in its plots.
Stori Ayers commands an excellent cast and thereby presents an excellent dramatic treatise on a never-ending American crisis.
It is a provocative and powerful closing to a play less concerned with the individual stories it tells and more focused on the stubborn, lasting narrative those stories evoke.

Her thought-provoking play – sometimes deadly earnest and sometimes surprisingly (but intentionally) hilarious under Stori Ayers’ accomplished direction – focuses on two strong-willed African-American women, born over 150 years apart, but both trying to attain their own version of “freedom.”
Handled with much less finesse is the easy symmetry of the past and the present stories presented here.
The play lacks some of the human interest that we find in Morisseau's other plays.

Dominique Morisseau’s Confederates, the second play of her Signature Theatre Residency 5, is a clever, but overly talky dissertation on race, power and family. She offers the audience parallel stories alternating between the Civil War era and modern day academia.
Director Stori Ayers skillfully navigates 'Confederates' between the satirical and the serious, and the rewards are great.
